content.text: What about Oxygen and Hydrogen? Let's talk about Oxidation and Reduction.

scenes.teacherScript: But what happens to Oxygen and Hydrogen during reactions? Let's talk about Oxidation and Reduction.

content.heading: Activity 1.11: Heating Copper
bullets: Heat about 1g of copper powder in a china dish.
The surface becomes coated with a black substance.
This black substance is Copper(II) oxide.

scenes.teacherScript: Let's look at an experiment. If you heat a china dish containing about 1 gram of copper powder, you'll observe that the surface of the copper powder becomes coated with a black substance. Why has this black substance formed? This is because oxygen from the air is added to the copper, forming copper(II) oxide.
The chemical equation for this is 2Cu plus O2 gives 2CuO. Here, oxygen is added to copper. When a substance gains oxygen during a reaction, it is said to be oxidised.

content.heading: Redox Reactions
bullets: Oxidation: Gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen.
Reduction: Loss of oxygen or gain of hydrogen.
Redox: One reactant gets oxidised while the other gets reduced.

scenes.teacherScript: Oxidation is simply the gain of oxygen, or the loss of hydrogen. Conversely, Reduction is the loss of oxygen, or the gain of hydrogen. These two usually happen side by side! If one reactant gets oxidised, the other gets reduced. Such reactions are called Oxidation-Reduction, or Redox reactions.

For example, when hydrogen gas is passed over heated Copper Oxide, the black coating turns brown as copper is obtained. The Copper Oxide loses oxygen, so it is reduced to copper. The hydrogen gains oxygen to form water, so it is oxidised. This is a classic Redox reaction!

content.text: Have you observed the effects of oxidation reactions in everyday life?

scenes.teacherScript: Now, you don't need a laboratory to see oxidation. Have you observed the effects of oxidation reactions in your everyday life? Let's look at Corrosion and Rancidity.

content.heading: Corrosion & Rancidity
bullets: Corrosion: Metal is attacked by moisture and air (e.g., Rusting of iron).
Rancidity: Fats and oils are oxidised, changing smell and taste.
Prevention: Add antioxidants or flush bags with Nitrogen.

scenes.teacherScript: When a metal is attacked by substances around it, like moisture or acids, it is said to corrode. Rusting of iron, the black coating on silver, and the green coating on copper are all examples of Corrosion, which causes massive damage to bridges and car bodies! Then we have Rancidity. When fats and oils are oxidised, they become rancid, and their smell and taste change. To prevent this, manufacturers add antioxidants to foods, or flush bags of chips with unreactive Nitrogen gas.
That covers the entire chapter! Let's do a quick comic recap to review some of these concepts.

messages.speaker: Rahul
messages.text: I still don't get it. Why do equations need to be balanced?

messages.speaker: Scientist Priya
messages.text: Because of the Law of Conservation of Mass! You can't create or destroy atoms, Rahul. If you put 5 atoms in, you must get exactly 5 atoms out!

messages.speaker: Oxygen Atom
messages.text: That's right! And when I jump onto a molecule, we call it Oxidation!

messages.speaker: Hydrogen Atom
messages.text: And when Oxygen leaves, it's Reduction. We like to do it together, creating a Redox Reaction!

messages.speaker: Rahul
messages.text: And what about all those color changes and heat we saw?

messages.speaker: Scientist Priya
messages.text: Those are signs of different reactions! Combination, Decomposition, Displacement, and Double Displacement. Plus, if it gets hot, it's Exothermic!
